questions.question: A research student spoke with two people, M and N, to learn about their work-related differences. The student concludes that while person M was working in an organised sector, person N was an employee of a workplace that was functioning in an unorganised way. Analyse the key differences between the two sectors that must have enabled the research student to come to this conclusion.
answer_steps: Regular vs irregular work: M has assured, regular work with fixed terms of employment; N's job is low-paid and often irregular, with no guarantee of continuous work.
Government regulation: M's enterprise is registered and follows laws such as the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act; N's workplace is largely outside government control, and rules are not followed.
Job security: M has security of employment and clear working hours; N can be dismissed without notice or reason, and work may stop in some seasons.
Benefits: M gets overtime pay, paid leave, holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and a pension; N gets no overtime, paid leave or medical benefits.
Working conditions: M's employer must provide a safe environment and facilities such as clean drinking water; N often works in unsafe conditions without legal protection.

questions.question: Privatisation can have both positive and negative effects on the economy. Support the statement with arguments.
answer_steps: Positive: privatisation can increase efficiency and productivity, since private firms are driven by competition and profit.
Positive: it can improve the quality of services and reduce the financial burden on the government.
Negative: with profit as the only motive, public welfare may be ignored, and essential services may not reach poor or remote people.
Negative: workers may lose employment security, and the gap between rich and poor may widen when basic facilities become costly.
Negative: private firms are less accountable to the public than the government; so a balance between public and private sectors is needed.

questions.question: Explain the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary sectors using examples other than those mentioned in the text.
answer_steps: Primary sector: produces goods by using natural resources directly, for example growing tea, catching prawns, or collecting tendu leaves.
Secondary sector: changes natural products into other forms through manufacturing, for example making tea powder in a factory, canning fish, or making furniture from timber.
Tertiary sector: provides services that support production and people, for example a courier service, a mobile phone repair shop, or a tuition teacher.

questions.question: Distinguish between open unemployment and disguised unemployment.
answer_steps: Open unemployment: a person who is able and willing to work has no job, and is clearly visible as unemployed.
Disguised unemployment: people appear to be working, but more people are working than needed; if some leave, production does not fall, as on small family farms.

questions.question: 'Tertiary sector is not playing any significant role in the development of the Indian economy.' Do you agree? Give reasons in support of your answer.
answer_steps: No, I do not agree: in 2013–14 the tertiary sector became the largest producing sector in India, replacing the primary sector.
It provides basic services such as hospitals, schools, banks, transport and communication, and supports agriculture and industry through transport, storage and trade.
New services based on information technology have grown fast; however, employment in this sector has not grown as much as production, and many service workers earn very little.

questions.question: Service sector in India employs two different kinds of people. Who are these?
answer_steps: Highly skilled and educated workers in well-paid services such as banking, IT, finance and professional services.
Workers in small-scale, low-paid services such as small shopkeepers, repair persons, street vendors and transport workers, who barely earn a living.

questions.question: Workers are exploited in the unorganised sector. Do you agree with this view? Give reasons in support of your answer.
answer_steps: Yes: jobs are low-paid and often irregular, and rules about wages and working conditions are not followed.
There is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or leave due to sickness, and no provident fund or pension.
Employment is not secure: workers can be asked to leave without any reason, and work slackens in some seasons.

questions.question: Compare the employment conditions prevailing in the organised and unorganised sectors.
answer_steps: Organised: enterprises are registered by the government and follow laws such as the Factories Act; unorganised: small and scattered units largely outside government control.
Organised: regular work, job security, fixed hours and overtime pay; unorganised: low-paid, irregular and insecure work with long hours and no overtime.
Organised: paid leave, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and pension; unorganised: none of these benefits.

questions.question: Explain the objective of implementing the MGNREGA 2005.
answer_steps: MGNREGA 2005 implements the Right to Work in rural India by guaranteeing 100 days of employment in a year to all who are able and in need of work.
If the government fails to give work, it pays an unemployment allowance; one-third of the jobs are reserved for women.
It gives preference to work that increases production from land, such as water conservation, so it also reduces disguised unemployment in villages.

questions.question: Give a few examples of public sector activities and explain why the government has taken them up.
answer_steps: Examples: railways, post offices, roads, bridges, dams for irrigation, electricity generation, schools and hospitals.
Many of these need very large spending that the private sector cannot afford, and it is not possible to collect money from thousands of users.
The government provides them at a reasonable cost so that they are available for everyone, and supports farmers and consumers, for example through the PDS.

questions.question: Explain how the public sector contributes to the economic development of a nation.
answer_steps: It provides infrastructure such as roads, railways, harbours, electricity and irrigation that the private sector would not provide at a reasonable cost.
It supplies electricity and other inputs at affordable rates to small industries and buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price, selling them cheaply through ration shops.
It provides health, education and nutrition for all, which builds human capital and reduces poverty and inequality.

questions.question: What are final goods and intermediate goods? Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
answer_steps: Final goods reach the consumer, like biscuits; intermediate goods are used up in making final goods, like wheat and flour.
Only final goods are counted because their value already includes the intermediate goods; counting both would be double counting.

questions.question: Distinguish between the public sector and the private sector.
answer_steps: Public sector: the government owns most assets and provides services, for public welfare, like Indian Railways.
Private sector: individuals or companies own assets and provide services, mainly for profit, like Reliance Industries.

questions.question: Why has employment not shifted out of the primary sector as much as production?
answer_steps: The secondary and tertiary sectors have not created enough jobs in proportion to their growth in production.
So nearly half of the workers remain in agriculture, leading to disguised unemployment.

questions.question: Why has the tertiary sector become the most important sector in India?
answer_steps: Basic services like hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts, banks and transport are needed, and the government provides many of them.
Development of agriculture and industry increases the demand for transport, trade and storage; and as incomes rise, people demand services like eating out, tourism and private schools.
New services based on information and communication technology have become important and have grown fast.

questions.question: Suggest ways to create more employment in rural areas.
answer_steps: Build dams and canals for irrigation, and improve roads, transport and storage, so that farmers can grow and sell more.
Give farmers cheap credit from banks, and set up agro-processing industries such as dal mills, cold storage and honey collection in semi-rural areas.
Expand education, health and tourism services, and implement schemes like MGNREGA, which guarantees 100 days of work.

questions.question: Why does the government take up some economic activities itself?
answer_steps: Some activities need very large spending, like roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity and dams, which the private sector cannot afford or will not provide at a reasonable cost.
The government supports small industries with affordable electricity, and supports farmers and consumers by buying grain at fair prices and selling it cheaply through ration shops.
Health, education and nutrition for all are primary responsibilities of the government.

questions.question: Explain the three sectors of the economy with examples, and show how they are interdependent.
answer_steps: Primary sector: produces goods by exploiting natural resources, such as agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry and mining; also called the agriculture and related sector.
Secondary sector: changes natural products into other forms through manufacturing, such as making cloth from cotton or sugar from sugarcane; also called the industrial sector.
Tertiary sector: provides services that support the other sectors and people, such as transport, storage, communication, banking, trade, teaching and IT; also called the service sector.
Interdependence: a sugar mill needs sugarcane from farmers, and if farmers stop selling, the mill shuts down; farmers need fertilisers and tools made in factories.
Both primary and secondary sectors need transport, storage, banking and trade from the tertiary sector to sell their products.

questions.question: Who are the workers in the unorganised sector, and why do they need protection? Suggest ways to protect them.
answer_steps: In rural areas, the unorganised sector includes landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans such as weavers, blacksmiths and carpenters.
In urban areas, it includes casual workers in small industry, construction, trade and transport, street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers and rag pickers.
They need protection because jobs are low-paid, irregular and insecure, with no paid leave, overtime, provident fund or pension, and rules are not followed.
The government should ensure fair wages, safety and health for these workers, and enforce laws like the Minimum Wages Act.
Small producers should get cheap credit and help in buying raw materials and marketing output, and schemes like MGNREGA can give rural workers assured work.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"Laxmi's family of five works on their small plot of land all through the year. Even if two members of the family move away to do some other work, the production on the plot will not be affected. In other words, more people are working than are actually needed. They are, in a sense, underemployed."* (Adapted from NCERT)

(i) What type of unemployment is described here? (1)

(ii) How is it different from open unemployment? (1)

(iii) Suggest two ways to reduce such unemployment. (2)
answer_steps: (i) Disguised unemployment (underemployment).
(ii) Here everyone appears to be working, but some are not needed; in open unemployment, a person clearly has no job.
(iii) Any two: irrigation through dams and canals; cheap credit for farmers; agro-processing industries in semi-rural areas; better transport and storage; MGNREGA works.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"The organised sector covers those enterprises or places of work where the terms of employment are regular and therefore, people have assured work. They are registered by the government and have to follow its rules and regulations which are given in various laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act, Shops and Establishments Act etc."* (NCERT)

(i) Why do workers in the organised sector have assured work? (1)

(ii) Name any one law that organised sector enterprises must follow. (1)

(iii) State two features of the unorganised sector. (2)
answer_steps: (i) Because the terms of employment are regular and the enterprises are registered and regulated by the government.
(ii) Any one: Factories Act; Minimum Wages Act; Payment of Gratuity Act; Shops and Establishments Act.
(iii) Any two: small and scattered units outside government control; low-paid and irregular jobs; no paid leave, overtime or holidays; no job security.
